    2 · Your first classifier¶

    In tutorial 1 we built a graph of twelve sentences. Now we use the 20 Newsgroups benchmark (one of the datasets of Yao et al., 2019 and Pereira & de Castro, DCAI 2022) and go all the way to test accuracy:

    1. Download it and write the Text4GCN input files.
    2. Preprocess it with TextPipeline.
    3. Build the graph with Frequency.tfidf().
    4. Train and evaluate a GCN with GNN.fit().

    Runtime: with the 4-category subset (~3.6k documents) this takes about 2.5 min on a T4 GPU and needs about 4 GB of RAM. Almost all of it is building the graph (about 2 min), which runs on the CPU; a GPU speeds up only the training, which takes several times longer on CPU.

    Configuration¶

    The whole corpus, documents and vocabulary, becomes a single graph. The full 20NG (18,846 posts) therefore needs a large GPU. We use the four categories of the classic scikit-learn text tutorial. To scale up, add categories or set CATEGORIES = None.

    In [4]:
    Copied! 
    NAME = "20NG4"
DATA_DIR = Path("data")
LOG_DIR = Path("logs")
SEED = 1234
CATEGORIES = ["alt.atheism", "soc.religion.christian", "comp.graphics", "sci.med"]
    NAME = "20NG4" DATA_DIR = Path("data") LOG_DIR = Path("logs") SEED = 1234 CATEGORIES = ["alt.atheism", "soc.religion.christian", "comp.graphics", "sci.med"]

    1. Download and write the input files¶

    twenty_newsgroups() downloads the corpus with scikit-learn (already a dependency) and keeps the official train/test split. It strips e-mail headers, signatures and quoted replies, so the model learns from the message body, and it drops posts left with fewer than 5 words. It then calls save_corpus(), which writes the two files every Text4GCN dataset needs:

    | File | One line per document | |---|---| | <name>.txt | the text, on a single line | | <name>.meta | <doc id>\t<train|test>\t<label> |

    We start from an empty folder: TextPipeline rewrites its own files, but outputs left by an older run, such as a graph built for another vocabulary, would stay next to them.

    In [5]:
    Copied! 
    shutil.rmtree(DATA_DIR, ignore_errors=True)
txt_path, meta_path = twenty_newsgroups(DATA_DIR, name=NAME, categories=CATEGORIES)

meta = pd.read_csv(meta_path, sep="\t", names=["id", "split", "label"])
meta.pivot_table(index="label", columns="split", values="id", aggfunc="count", margins=True)
    shutil.rmtree(DATA_DIR, ignore_errors=True) txt_path, meta_path = twenty_newsgroups(DATA_DIR, name=NAME, categories=CATEGORIES) meta = pd.read_csv(meta_path, sep="\t", names=["id", "split", "label"]) meta.pivot_table(index="label", columns="split", values="id", aggfunc="count", margins=True)

    2. Preprocess¶

    execute() writes three folders next to the input files:

    Folder Content
    <name>.cleaned/ text lower-cased and tokenized, without stop words and words seen fewer than rare_count times
    <name>.shuffled/ documents shuffled with seed, the vocabulary, the train/test ids
    <name>.node_features/ feature and label matrices; validation_ratio of the training documents is held out for validation

    validation_ratio is the only place where the validation split is defined.

    In [7]:
    Copied! 
    TextPipeline(
    dataset_name=NAME,
    dataset_path=DATA_DIR,
    rare_count=5,
    language="english",
    seed=SEED,
).execute(validation_ratio=0.10)
    TextPipeline( dataset_name=NAME, dataset_path=DATA_DIR, rare_count=5, language="english", seed=SEED, ).execute(validation_ratio=0.10)

    3. Build the graph¶

    The TextGCN graph has PMI word–word edges and TF-IDF document–word edges (see tutorial 1). GraphBuildStats reports its size.

    In [9]:
    Copied! 
    stats = Frequency(dataset_name=NAME, dataset_path=DATA_DIR).tfidf(window_size=20)
stats
    stats = Frequency(dataset_name=NAME, dataset_path=DATA_DIR).tfidf(window_size=20) stats
    text4gcn · Frequency.tfidf("20NG4") · window 20
  ✓ graph     14,537 nodes · 4.53 M edges (4.26 M word–word) · density 2.15% · 52.0 MiB  (2m02s)
    Out[9]:
    GraphBuildStats(builder='frequency.tfidf', dataset='20NG4', nodes=14,537, edges=4,534,779, word_word=4,258,440, density=2.15%, size='52.0 MiB')

    4. Train and evaluate¶

    GNN loads the features and the graph and trains a 2-layer GCN with the protocol of the paper: hidden size 200, dropout 0.5 and learning rate 0.02. Training stops early when the validation loss rises above its mean over the previous 10 epochs (the criterion of the reference TextGCN code). It uses CUDA when available. When training stops, the weights with the best validation loss are restored and evaluated on the test documents.

    In [10]:
    Copied! 
    result = GNN(
    dataset_name=NAME,
    dataset_path=DATA_DIR,
    log_dir=LOG_DIR,
    builder=Builder.Tfidf,      # the graph built in step 3
    seed=SEED,
).fit()
    result = GNN( dataset_name=NAME, dataset_path=DATA_DIR, log_dir=LOG_DIR, builder=Builder.Tfidf, # the graph built in step 3 seed=SEED, ).fit()

    Training curves are saved in log_dir.

    The loss values stay close to $\ln(4) \approx 1.39$, and the validation curve looks almost flat. This is expected: as in the reference TextGCN implementation, the cross-entropy is averaged over all nodes, and the rows outside each split have zeroed logits. Accuracy is the curve to read.
